title: Faith that moves mountains (Mark 11:20–25)
hook: have faith in God, and when you pray, forgive

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fig tree and the temple, and your line was a house of prayer for all. Who did you make room for? Day two hundred eight.

Next morning, the same road in from Bethany. They pass yesterday's fig tree, and it's dried up from the roots. Peter remembers, and points, a little stunned. In the King James Bible: "Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away." You can hear him wanting an explanation. What was that about? What does it mean? What was the lesson? And Jesus doesn't talk about fig trees at all. He doesn't explain the temple either. He starts talking about prayer, and about a mountain. And then, when you'd expect him to finish with something grand, he ends somewhere very small and very close to home. Somewhere most of us would rather not go.
screen: `THE SAME ROAD, NEXT MORNING.` → `WITHERED FROM THE ROOTS.` → `WHAT DOES IT MEAN?`

segments.voice: Jesus says three words: "Have faith in God." Then the big picture: whoever says to this mountain, be lifted up and thrown into the sea, and doesn't doubt in their heart, it will happen. They're walking near the Mount of Olives, within sight of the temple mount. Moving a mountain was a way of saying doing the impossible; later Jewish teachers praised a brilliant rabbi as an uprooter of mountains. Then he goes further: whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. This is a verse people have leaned on and argued over. Some Christians hear a bold promise to pray big. Others warn against treating it like a vending machine, and read it next to other places where Jesus prays that God's will be done. Most churches hold both: pray boldly, and trust. But here's the turn almost nobody quotes on a poster. The very next sentence: "And when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any: that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses." Right after the mountain, the condition isn't more faith. It's forgiveness. Before you ask for mountains to move, let go of the grudge. The Greek word for forgive means to release, to let go, like opening your hand and dropping something. It's the same word used for leaving nets by the lake. The fig tree without fruit, the temple without prayer, and now this: the fruit Jesus is looking for might start with a grudge you finally put down. The mountain that won't move may be the one inside.
screen: `HAVE FAITH IN GOD.` · `A MOUNTAIN INTO THE SEA.` · `PRAY BOLDLY, AND TRUST.` · `WHEN YE STAND PRAYING, FORGIVE.` · then, large: `WHEN YE STAND PRAYING, FORGIVE, IF YE HAVE OUGHT AGAINST ANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive first. Settle, and breathe. Is there someone you have ought against, as the old English says? Someone you're holding something against, big or small? Let their face come to mind. You don't have to feel warm. You don't have to pretend it didn't matter, or call them. Just picture opening your hand, and letting the grudge drop, even for these two minutes. If you pray, you can do that first, and then bring your prayer. If you don't, just notice what your hand feels like, open. The bell holds the time.
Faith that moves mountains. Pray boldly, trust God, and before you ask, forgive.
Your line: forgive, then pray. Today, whenever you ask for something, from God or from anyone, check your hand first for a grudge. Day two hundred eight.

howItsDone: Many Christians examine their hearts and forgive others before praying, and many churches exchange a sign of peace before communion, echoing Jesus's words that forgiveness comes before prayer.

myth: Jesus explains what the fig tree meant
he doesn't; he talks about faith, prayer and forgiveness.
the promise about mountains ends with forgiveness
moving mountains was a way of saying doing the impossible
later Jewish teachers called a great rabbi an uprooter of mountains.

fork.setup: you've just heard that faith can move a mountain. what's the very next thing Jesus says to do when you pray?
options: forgive anyone you hold something against.
fork.reveal: "when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any." the mountain, then the grudge.

original.note: Greek: forgive, let go, release. from aphiēmi, also used for leaving nets behind.

trapdoor: what you thought: enough faith gets you whatever you want.
what it means: pray boldly and trust God, and before you pray, forgive.
what a scholar hears: aphiēmi means to release. and verse 26 in the King James is missing from the oldest manuscripts.

sources.quoted: Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away.
And when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any: that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses.

notes: 'Uprooter of mountains' (oker harim) as praise of a sharp rabbi: Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 64a (and elsewhere). It is later than the Gospels; the script says 'later Jewish teachers'. Confirm.
Mark 11:26 absent from the earliest manuscripts; confirm.
'The same word used for leaving nets' refers to aphiēmi in Mark 1:18. Confirm.
Readings of 11:24 (bold prayer vs. a 'vending machine' view) kept general and unranked.
